Model decomposition for serving-aware evaluations

SUMMARY:
This playbook describes a recommended, repeatable process to decompose large monolithic models into serving-aware subcomponents for evaluation. The goal is to make evals, quantization checks, and regression triage reflect the real production serving stack (tokenization, adapter layers, kv-cache behavior, quant kernels, and network shims) so that performance, quality, and rollback decisions are grounded in operational reality rather than idealized model binaries.

CONTENTS:
- Motivation and scope
- Decomposition strategy and component contracts
- Evaluation harness integration patterns
- Quantization compatibility matrix and validations
- Onboarding checklist and promotion gates
- Regression triage adjustments and runbook
- Example manifests and CLI examples

1) MOTIVATION AND SCOPE
Decomposing models into serving-aware components reduces blind spots that cause regressions during rollouts. Typical blind spots include: quantized kernel mismatches, tokenizer differences, KV cache truncation, and custom adapter layers that change attention shape. This doc applies to:
- Large decoder-only or encoder-decoder models being promoted to Redwood hosted/dedicated/private runtime.
- Model variants (FP16, 4-bit/Quantized, adapter-fused versions).
- Evals that must simulate realistic per-request state (KV-cache warm/cold, streaming chunk sizes, prefix-caching).

2) DECOMPOSITION STRATEGY
High-level decomposition targets the following components:
- Tokenizer layer (tokenize/normalize/encoder mapping)
- Front-end adapters (prompt prep, input filters, instruction wrappers)
- Core model weight blob (architecture + weights)
- KV-cache/serving-state shim (serialization format + truncation policy)
- Quantization/exec profile (kernel selection, op-fusion knobs)
- Network shim (protocol differences: gRPC vs HTTP/streaming)
- Post-processing (detokenization, response filters, function-call wiring)

Batching, Cache Cohesion, and Eviction: Platform Roadmap 2025

Summary:

This roadmap defines the 2025 initiative to unify and harden our request batching, KV/prefix cache cohesion, and eviction policies across the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to reduce per-token cost by 18–30% for typical multi-tenant workloads, hold 99th-percentile latency SLOs, and provide deterministic operator controls for capacity events and spot/burst usage.

Context and motivation:

- Current state: The serving runtime supports continuous batching and a prefix/KV cache, but batching heuristics, cache sharding, and eviction behaviors are implemented in multiple places and tuned per-service. This causes unpredictable tail latency under mixed-sequence-length workloads and uneven cost distribution between tenants.
- Business drivers: Lower unit cost for hosted inference, clearer tenant billing signals, fewer incidents related to cache thrash and eviction storms, and simpler migration path to Dedicated/Private deployments.

Goals (measurable):

1. Cost: Reduce median per-token GPU cost by 18% and P95 per-token cost by 25% for our top-10 multi-tenant workloads within six months of rollout.
2. Latency: Preserve 99th-percentile latency SLOs for interactive (<300ms target) workloads; maintain P95 <= 120ms where current baseline is <120ms.
3. Observability: Deliver dedicated dashboards and alerting for batch composition, cache hit/miss by prefix, eviction rate, and tenant-level token-cost drift within the first quarter.
4. Operational controls: Implement operator-level throttles, graceful eviction deltas, and fast rollback switches with documented runbooks.

Design principles:

- Workload-aware heuristics: Batching decisions should use historical sequence-length distributions per route/tenant to avoid prefix padding that increases cost.

Contributor Onboarding and Lint Pipeline for Docs Site

Overview:
This playbook documents the recommended contributor onboarding flow for the Docs Site repository, plus the continuous integration (CI) lint pipeline and local checks every contributor should run before submitting a PR. The goal is to reduce authoring friction, lower review cycles, and keep the docs site fast and correct for customers.

Who this is for:
- New documentation contributors (engineers, product, and technical writers)
- Maintainers and reviewers of the docs-site repo
- Developer experience (DevX) and DX tools engineers

High-level goals:
1) Make new contributors productive in < 2 hours.
2) Block common formatting, link, and snippet regressions at CI time.
3) Provide a reproducible local pre-commit checklist for fast feedback.

Ownership and contact:
- Maintainers: eng-developer-experience/docs-site team (primary contact: @maya.torres)
- CI pipeline owner: @ravi.patel (DevX infra)
- Escalation: docs-site-maintainers Slack channel (#docs-site)

Quickstart: first PR in 6 steps
1. Fork the repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/docs-site.git && cd docs-site
2. Bootstrap local environment: ./scripts/bootstrap.sh (see Appendix A for expected dependencies)
3. Run the pre-commit hooks: pre-commit run --all-files
4. Create a feature branch: git checkout -b fix/snippet-typo-<issue#>
5. Make edits and run local checks: ./scripts/check-all.sh
6. Push and open PR using the docs PR template: https://github.com/redwood-inference/docs-site/.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md

Pipeline overview (what CI enforces)
- Stage: lint-format
  - Tools: prettier, markdownlint, remark-lint (config in .remarkrc)
  - Checks: trailing whitespace, heading levels, line length exceptions, consistent code fence languages
- Stage: links-and-assets
  - Tools: htmlproofer (site build mode), custom link-checker
  - Checks: broken internal links, missing image assets, mismatched anchors across versions

Summary:
This playbook defines a product-centric approach to map serving SLOs to customer-facing pricing tiers and consumption controls. It combines quantitative SLO bands, cost-to-serve estimates, and operational rollout guidance for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. The goal is to make pricing predictable, align incentives for efficiency, and provide a clear migration path for customers who need higher SLOs (latency, availability, and throughput).

Goals and non-goals:

  - Specify rollout and gating criteria for migrating customers between tiers.

Key definitions and metrics:
- Latency P95: 95th percentile end-to-end token latency per request (ms).
- Availability: Percentage of successful token-serving requests excluding client errors.
- Throughput: sustained tokens/sec per tenant during a 5-minute window.
- Unit: 1 generation token (unweighted) and 1 embedding operation (separate metric).
- Error budget: 1 - Availability_target; used for gating migrations and rollouts.

This document defines the API-driven synthetic telemetry and local service-stub contract used across Redwood Inference for: local development, preflight integration tests, controlled synthetic load generation, and gated model-serving rollout checks.
